title: Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: Chapter 7: Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
question: What growth and margin does today's price already assume, and how do peers price a similar story?

epigraph.quote: What is a cynic? A man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing.
epigraph.author: Oscar Wilde, Lady Windermere's Fan (1892)

web_blocks.html: On 13 November 2026 Proventus Agrocom closed at ₹2,125.70, a new 52-week high, which values the equity at ₹734.1 crore on 34,53,416 shares [71][21]. The 12 November ledger close was ₹2,061.00, or ₹711.7 crore. We use ₹2,125.70 as the current price and name both closes where the gap matters. One fact outranks every multiple here. The H1 FY27 results were filed at about 17:57 IST on 13 November, after the 15:30 close [1][2]. Neither close reflects them, and the first chance to react is Monday 16 November. Every multiple below pairs a price set without the news with earnings that include it.

Over the twelve months to September 2026 the group booked ₹1,168.3 crore of revenue and ₹19.24 crore of profit after tax [1][3]. That trailing profit adds H2 FY26 EPS of ₹21.75 to H1 FY27 EPS of ₹33.96, giving ₹55.71. TradingView still shows 52.04x because its feed has not yet taken in the new half-year [71]. On FY2026 EPS of ₹40.95 the multiple is 51.9x (the half-year figures in the table below add to ₹40.99 because the Screener half-year EPS values are rounded). On trailing EPS that includes H1 FY27 it is 38.2x, or 37.0x at the 12 November close. The half-year that left the window earned EPS of ₹19.24 and the one that replaced it earned ₹33.96, so trailing EPS rose 36% in one step and the multiple fell with no change in price.

web_blocks.html: Two readings carry the weight. A price of 0.63x sales sounds modest, but a business that keeps 1.65 paise of profit per rupee of sales has little room for error, and 31x EV to EBITDA says the market pays for growth and not for today's margin. The second signal is a 10.3% ROE against 4.7x book value. An investor who needs 14% a year is paying a large premium for a business that earns about 10% on its equity. That is justified only if returns rise as the base grows, which Chapter 6 showed has not yet happened.

PROV listed in June 2023, so its history is short, and every observation sits on a thin tape with a median of 320 shares a day [73]. We divided each half-year-end price by trailing EPS at that date. The result is a band, not a verdict, because the denominator was tiny for most of the period.

web_blocks.caption: Price at half-year end divided by trailing-12-month EPS
web_blocks.takeaway: Prices from the Yahoo Finance history [73]; EPS from audited and limited-review results [3][1]; our calculation. Minimum 28.9x, median 45.4x, maximum 64.6x.

web_blocks.html: Today's 38.2x sits below the 45.4x median and above the 28.9x floor, so on its own history the stock is not stretched. The comparison flatters less than it seems. The 60x-plus readings came when EPS was about ₹21, so small changes in profit moved the multiple a long way. The 28.9x low came in March 2026, after trailing EPS jumped 54% in six months. Since March 2024 the price is up 119% while trailing EPS is up 160%. Earnings have run ahead of price, which is healthy, but the next gain must come from growth on a much larger base.

web_blocks.title: What the price already assumes: a reverse earnings test

web_blocks.html: A reverse test asks what must be true for today's price to earn a fair return. We compound the market capitalisation for five years at the required return and divide by the P/E a buyer might pay in year five. The answer is the profit the business must then earn. We treat 14% and 20x as the central pairing, because a ₹700 crore company with a 2% margin should not be assumed to hold a premium multiple forever.

web_blocks.caption: Year-five profit after tax needed to earn the required return from ₹734.1 crore (implied annual growth from trailing ₹19.24 crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Our calculation (valuation.py) from the market capitalisation at ₹2,125.70 and trailing PAT of ₹19.24 Cr [1][3]. Dilution is ignored, which understates the hurdle.

web_blocks.html: At the central pairing the company must earn ₹70.7 crore in year five, which is 3.7 times today's trailing profit and a compound growth rate of 29.7%. PAT did rise from ₹3.7 crore in FY2023 to ₹14.3 crore in FY2026 [15][3], but from a tiny base, and the hurdle applies for five straight years. Management guides brand revenue to ₹850 crore in FY27 and ₹1,100 crore in FY28, near 29% growth [3][5]. So the price assumes management meets its own guide for five years and holds the net margin where it is. It leaves almost no slack for a slower path.

web_blocks.caption: Revenue and margin needed for ₹70.7 crore of year-five profit, and the working capital that growth absorbs
headers: Working capital at 12-15% of extra revenue
web_blocks.takeaway: Our calculation from trailing revenue of ₹1,168.3 Cr and a net margin of about 1.65% [1][3]; 12-15% brackets Chapter 6's 11.6% (March) and 16.0% (September).

web_blocks.html: The funding column is the real finding. On the required path the business earns only about ₹224 crore of cumulative profit over five years. Growth of 25% to 30% needs ₹288 to ₹475 crore of extra working capital, so the difference must come from banks or new shares. Borrowings already rose from ₹27.0 crore to ₹56.4 crore in H1 FY27 [3][1]. This matches Chapter 6's estimate that own cash earnings fund about 14% growth a year. Growth of 20% asks for a 2.43% margin, some 78 bps above today's. Growth of 30% asks for no margin gain but the most capital. Each path rests on something the record has not shown.

web_blocks.title: How the peers price a similar story

web_blocks.html: No listed company matches PROV. The closest are branded food names: Bikaji (snacks), LT Foods (rice), Tata Consumer (tea and staples), KRBL (rice) and Prataap Snacks. The table uses same-session TradingView fields [72]; DFM Foods returned no data. PROV's P/E here is the pre-H1 52.0x; with H1 FY27 it is 38.2x.

web_blocks.caption: PROV and listed food peers: same-session valuation, profitability and technical snapshot
web_blocks.takeaway: Prataap Snacks' 596.5x multiple reflects near-zero earnings and is not meaningful. PROV's market cap in this table, ₹710.36 Cr, is TradingView's figure and implies about 33.4 lakh shares; the text uses ₹734.1 Cr from the 34,53,416 shares in the shareholding filing. Peers differ in scale, mix and brand strength, so the table frames the multiple and does not set a fair value.

web_blocks.html: PROV's pre-H1 multiple is more than double LT Foods' 22.5x, although its operating margin is 1.86% against 8.21%, less than a quarter as much. Its ROE of 10.3% also trails LT Foods' 14.4%. Bikaji trades at 48.7x with a 9.48% margin and Tata Consumer at 62.8x with a 10.98% margin. KRBL earns 16.13% and trades at 11.7x because its revenue is flat. Divide each multiple by revenue growth and PROV (52.0x on +59%) looks much like LT Foods (22.5x on +24.3%). The difference is quality: LT Foods turns each rupee of sales into more than four times the operating profit. PROV pays a growth premium that its margin has not yet earned.

Private dry-fruit brands show why the market pays it. Farmley neared ₹400 crore of FY25 revenue with losses under control, and Happilo's revenue fell 15% to ₹280 crore while it cut losses by 93% [46][47]. A nut brand that is profitable and grows 59% is unusual, and that scarcity is part of the price.

web_blocks.title: Where we think fair value sits

web_blocks.html: Our value comes from the scenario set that Chapter 9 develops. The price in twelve months, about November 2027, equals trailing EPS at September 2027 multiplied by an exit P/E. In the base case, revenue grows 35% in H2 FY27 at a 1.6% net margin and 30% in H1 FY28 at 1.8%, which gives trailing EPS of ₹76.4. The bear case gives ₹47.6 and the bull case ₹102.7. The exit multiple is the swing factor.

The answer is highly sensitive to a number nobody can know. On base EPS of ₹76.4, an exit multiple of 22x gives ₹1,681 (-20.9%), 29x gives ₹2,216 (+4.2%) and 38x gives ₹2,903 (+36.6%). That swing of ₹1,222 a share is 57% of today's price, with no change in earnings. We chose 29x because it is about 0.76 of today's 38.2x, a PEG near 0.78 on 37% base-case EPS growth, and the low end of PROV's own band. Growth should slow from the trailing +92%, and cash conversion is unproven. A buyer who trusts the margin story would pay 33x or more; a doubter would pay 22x.

web_blocks.caption: Scenario values and what a buyer at today's price earns
web_blocks.takeaway: Our scenarios; the last column divides each value by 1.14, the required return used in the reverse test.

web_blocks.html: The probability-weighted price of ₹2,174 is only 2.3% above ₹2,125.70. An investor who needs 14% a year would find ₹2,125.70 about 9% above the ₹1,944 that the base case supports today and 11.5% above the ₹1,907 of the weighted case. The stock is priced for the base case with no cushion. The TradingView-based snapshot tags it Reasonable and In-line [71]; our reading is fair to full, with the margin of safety missing.

web_blocks.the_number: Fair value of about ₹1,900 to ₹1,950 a share today for an investor who needs 14% a year. In November 2027 the base case is ₹2,216.
web_blocks.how_calculated: Base-case trailing EPS at September 2027 (₹76.4) times a 29x exit P/E gives ₹2,216. Dividing by 1.14 gives ₹1,944 today. The probability-weighted ₹2,174 divided by 1.14 gives ₹1,907.
web_blocks.the_inputs: H1 FY27 EPS ₹33.96 and H2 FY26 EPS ₹21.75 [1][3]; 34,53,416 shares [21]; base growth of 35% and 30% at net margins of 1.6% and 1.8%; PROV's own P/E band of 28.9x to 64.6x [73]; peer multiples [72].
web_blocks.the_range: On base EPS, exit multiples of 22x to 38x give ₹1,681 to ₹2,903 in November 2027, or ₹1,475 to ₹2,546 in today's money at 14%. Across all three cases the spread is ₹952 to ₹3,902.
web_blocks.if_off: If receivables fall and operating cash flow turns positive, the multiple is more likely to hold near 33x to 38x. If receivables stay above ₹75 crore with negative cash flow, 22x or lower is likelier and the base case is too generous.

web_blocks.html: Valuation therefore says that ₹2,125.70 is a fair price for a good outcome and a poor price for an ordinary one. Two limits apply. The H1 FY27 figures are unaudited and limited-reviewed, and Monday's trade will reset the multiples [1]. Every historical price sits on a thin SME tape. The entry price has to carry the margin of safety that the multiple does not: the ₹1,944 and ₹1,907 values sit 3.7% and 1.7% above the ₹1,875 top of our ₹1,850 to ₹1,875 zone. Chapter 8 reads the tape for a better price, and Chapter 9 sets the levels.

book_paragraphs: Let's start with the price on the screen, because it is the one number nobody argues about. On Friday 13 November the stock closed at ₹2,125.70. Multiply by 34.5 lakh shares and the market is saying this company is worth ₹734 crore. Now ask yourself what that figure is actually buying. Over the last twelve months the group sold about ₹1,168 crore of goods and kept ₹19 crore of it. That is a bit more than one and a half paise of profit on every rupee. You are paying 38 times that profit, and the question for the next hour is whether you are being asked to pay for what the company is, or for what you hope it will be.

I want you to hold one fact in your head before we touch a single multiple. The company filed its half-year results at about 17:57 that evening, more than two hours after the market closed. So ₹2,125.70 is the price of a stock whose buyers had not seen the numbers. The first trade that reflects them happens on Monday. Anything I tell you about valuation today is a photograph taken just before the news arrived, and you should treat it that way.

Here is the first surprise. The screen on most data terminals says the stock trades at 52 times earnings. That figure is old. When we add the new half-year, trailing earnings per share jump from about ₹41 to ₹55.71, because the six months that dropped out earned ₹19 a share and the six that replaced them earned nearly ₹34. The price did not move; the multiple fell to 38. This is the quiet trick of a fast-growing company. It looks expensive on yesterday's profit and merely full on today's, and what you pay for depends on which day's profit you believe.

So how does 38 compare with the company's own past? Since listing, I find a band from about 29 to about 65 times, with a middle near 45. We are inside it, below the middle. That sounds comforting until you notice that most of the very high readings came when earnings were tiny. A company that earns ₹21 a share can show 60 times with almost any price. Today the earnings base is two and a half times larger, and the stock has still more than doubled since March 2024. Earnings have run faster than the price. That is the good news. The cost is that you can no longer expect the multiple to rescue you; the next gain has to be earned by growth.

Now the question I find most useful, the one that turns valuation into a story you can test. If you buy at today's price and want to earn 14% a year for five years, what must the company earn in year five? Assume a buyer then pays 20 times profit. The answer is about ₹71 crore, almost four times today's profit. That is growth of roughly 30% a year, every year, for five years. Management's own guide for brand revenue is close to 29%. So the price is a bet that the company hits its own plan and keeps today's thin margin. Nothing in that bet is impossible. It simply leaves no room for a slow year.

And here is where the cash comes in, and I hope Chapter 6 is still fresh. To grow revenue by 25% a year for five years, the company has to finance about ₹290 to ₹360 crore of extra stock and receivables. On that path it earns about ₹224 crore of profit in total. The gap must be filled by bank loans or new shares. Debt has already doubled in six months, from ₹27 crore to ₹56 crore. The CEO's letter says, in his words, that growth requires “the ability to convert earnings into healthy cash flows over time.” I agree entirely. The test is not what the company earns but what it keeps.

Let's look at the neighbours. LT Foods, the basmati and packaged-rice company, trades near 22 times earnings with an operating margin above 8%. Bikaji, the snacks company, trades near 49 times with a margin near 9.5%. Tata Consumer is above 60 times with a margin near 11%. PROV, with a margin under 2%, trades at 38 to 52 times. When you divide each multiple by sales growth, PROV and LT Foods look similar. What differs is what a rupee of sales turns into. At LT Foods it is more than four times the operating profit. The market is paying PROV for growth and for a rare thing among nut brands, which is profit at all. The private brands I looked at lose money. That scarcity is genuinely worth something. It just isn't worth everything.

So where do I think fair value sits? I will give you a range and not a point, because honesty demands it. In our base case the company earns trailing ₹76 a share by September 2027. Apply 29 times and you get ₹2,216, which is 4% above today. Apply 22 times and you get ₹1,681; apply 38 and you get ₹2,903. That swing of ₹1,222 a share comes entirely from a multiple that nobody can know. Weighing the bear, base and bull outcomes at 30, 50 and 20 percent gives ₹2,174, only 2% above the market. For an investor who wants 14% a year, the base case supports roughly ₹1,900 to ₹1,950 today.

Put differently, you are being offered a fair price for a good outcome. “Price is what you pay; value is what you get,” the old line goes, and the gap between the two is your margin of safety. At ₹2,125.70 that gap is thin; the base target sits only 4% above it. At ₹1,875, the top of our entry zone, the base target is about 18% higher, and the price sits 1.7% to 3.7% under what a 14% investor can justify. That is not a call to buy or sell yet; Chapter 9 does that with the full evidence. For now, remember the shape of the problem: the business is improving, the price already knows it, and the next move depends on a half-year result the market has not yet read.

One more thing, because I would be shortchanging you otherwise. Everything I have said rests on a stock that trades a few hundred shares on an ordinary day. A price discovered that thinly can be right, but it can also be an average of a handful of opinions. When you see a band of 29 to 65 times, remember that each point in it is a half-year-end print on a tape where a fifth of the sessions in the last year saw no trade at all. I give the band weight, and I do not give it authority.

Think of the whole chapter as three questions you can ask of any small company with a big story. What does the price assume? How much capital does that assumption consume? And what do I pay if the story is only mostly true? For this company the answers are: about 30% growth for five years; more capital than the business earns; and roughly ₹1,900 to ₹1,950 for a base case that I do not think is generous. Keep those three questions beside you when we read the tape in the next chapter.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A multiple is a conversation between what a company earns and what you believe it will earn. Today that conversation is mostly about the future, because the profit being capitalised is small and the growth being promised is large. When a price leaves no room for disappointment, the discipline is not to argue about whether the story is true. It is to ask what you would pay if the story were only mostly true.
